title: Job Control
lead: Manage shell jobs in the foreground or background, cancel with Ctrl+C, pause with Ctrl+Z, and use nohup when appropriate.
objectives: You distinguish foreground, background, and stopped shell jobs.
You manage the current terminal's jobs with `jobs`, `bg`, and `fg`.
You understand what `nohup` does and what it does not replace.

sections.title: Foreground, Ctrl+C, and Ctrl+Z
body: A foreground command occupies the terminal. `Ctrl+C` usually sends SIGINT to cancel it; `Ctrl+Z` sends SIGTSTP and **pauses** the job. A stopped job is not finished and may still hold resources.
Adding `&` to the end of a command starts it in the background. That does not make it independent of the terminal; closing the session can still affect it.

commands.what: Waits for five minutes in the foreground and keeps the terminal busy.
commands.where: To safely try how a foreground job behaves.
commands.why: It demonstrates the difference between Ctrl+C and Ctrl+Z.

commands.what: Starts the sleep command in the background.
commands.where: When you want to keep entering commands in the terminal.
commands.why: The shell prints a job number and PID.

sections.tip: Do not forget a stopped job: find it with `jobs -l` and resume or stop it according to its purpose.

sections.title: jobs, bg, and fg
body: `jobs -l` lists jobs only in the current shell session. `bg %1` resumes a job in the background; `fg %1` brings it to the foreground. `%1` is the shell job number from `jobs`, not a PID.
A background job may continue writing to the terminal. The shell reports when it finishes. Do not guess the job number; check `jobs` first.

commands.what: Lists the current shell's jobs with their states and PIDs.
commands.where: When looking for stopped or background jobs.
commands.why: You can see the job number and state before choosing the correct job.

commands.what: Resumes a selected job in the background or brings it to the foreground.
commands.where: When resuming a job or reclaiming terminal control.
commands.why: It changes how the same job interacts with the terminal.

sections.tip: `jobs` gives the job number; `ps` or `jobs -l` shows the PID. They are not interchangeable.

sections.title: Session independence: nohup
body: `nohup` starts a command so that it ignores SIGHUP, which can help it continue after a session closes. A common pattern redirects output to a file and starts the command with `&`.

`nohup` is not a job monitor or service manager. Use `systemd` for long-running production services; use `tmux` or `screen` for interactive work across disconnected SSH sessions. Stop test jobs and inspect their output.

commands.what: Protects the command from SIGHUP, redirects output to a file, and starts it in the background.
commands.where: When a short, non-interactive job needs to outlive a session.
commands.why: Terminal output is retained and the shell is freed.

commands.what: Shows the job's most recent output lines.
commands.where: When checking progress or error messages.
commands.why: You can inspect the log without bringing the job to the foreground.

sections.warn: Test only in your own VM with a short job. `nohup` does not stop the job automatically; track its PID and log file.

vm.intro: Run the examples in your own test VM. A shell job belongs to that shell session; stop test jobs you no longer need.

v01.title: Stop a job
v01.text: Start `sleep` in the foreground. Press `Ctrl+Z` while it runs, then check the shell job with the command below.
differs: The job number may not be 1; use your own `jobs -l` output.
Make sure your terminal emulator sends Ctrl+Z to the shell.

v02.title: Background and clean up
v02.text: First verify the job number with `jobs -l`. Replace `%1` in the example with the correct number, resume it in the background, and then clean it up.
differs: Replace `%1` if your job number is different.
`kill %1` signals this shell job; use it only for the test `sleep` job.

v03.title: A short nohup job
v03.text: Redirect the output of a short command with `nohup`, wait for it to finish, and read the file.

blocks.cmd:
nohup sh -c 'sleep 2; echo done' > ~/job-output.txt 2>&1 &
sleep 3
cat ~/job-output.txt

differs: If the command is still running, wait a few seconds and run `cat ~/job-output.txt` again.
If you get a path or permission error, make sure the destination is inside your home directory.

q1.q: What does `Ctrl+Z` do to a running job?
q1.explain: Ctrl+Z usually sends SIGTSTP; the job pauses but is not complete.

q2.explain: The percent-prefixed number is the shell job number shown by `jobs`.

options: Turns the job into a systemd service
q3.explain: nohup starts a command to ignore SIGHUP; it is not a service manager by itself.

q4.q: What is the difference between a job number and a PID?
options: The job number belongs to the shell; the PID belongs to the process
A PID exists only for background jobs
q4.explain: A shell job number belongs to the current session; a PID identifies the system process.

summary: `Ctrl+C` usually cancels a job; `Ctrl+Z` pauses it.
`jobs`, `bg`, and `fg` manage the current shell's jobs; `%N` is a shell job number.
`nohup` protects against SIGHUP but does not replace a service manager; redirect output and monitor the job.

glossary.meaning: An interactive job that owns terminal control.
A job running in the shell without terminal control.
A signal processes may receive when a session or terminal connection closes.
